summary: Sets out requirements for trust anchor management. A trust anchor is an authoritative entity represented by a public key plus data that limits what it is trusted for, which a relying party uses to validate digitally signed objects. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A trust anchor is a public key that a device has been told to trust, together with rules about what that key may be trusted for. This RFC sets out what a protocol for installing and updating those keys would have to do, because today every application manages its own list in its own way.

questions: why is trust anchor management needed
how to manage trust anchors securely
subtitle: What a protocol for installing and updating a device's list of trusted keys would have to do.

tldr.problem: Every device holds a list of public keys it trusts, and there is no standard way to find out what is in that list or to change it, so each application rolls its own.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a trust anchor as a public key plus data constraining what it is trusted for, and lists requirements for a push-based protocol that manages stores of them.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document. The format and the protocol it points at were published separately, as RFC 5914 and RFC 5934.

facts.label: Trust anchor contents required
facts.value: A public key, a public key algorithm and, if necessary, parameters

facts.label: Out-of-band checks

Recovery from a lost key

sections.title: What a Trust Anchor Is
sections.content:
Digital signatures are used in many applications. For them to give integrity and authentication, the public key used to verify the signature must be trusted, that is, accepted by a relying party as appropriate for use in the given context. A public key used to verify a signature must either be configured as a trust anchor, or be contained in a certificate that can be transitively verified by a certification path ending at a trust anchor.

A trust anchor is a public key plus associated data used by a relying party to validate a signature on a signed object, where that object is either a public key certificate that begins a certification path terminated by a signature or encryption certificate, or an object other than a public key certificate or certificate revocation list that cannot be validated through a certification path. The associated data defines the scope of the trust anchor by constraining the signatures it may be used to verify; if a trust anchor verifies X.509 certificates, those constraints might include name spaces, certificate policies, or application and usage types.

Trust anchors have only local significance: each relying party is configured with a set of trust anchors, either by itself or by an entity that manages them in the context it operates in. The RFC defines three terms. A trust anchor store is a set of one or more trust anchors stored in a device; a store may be managed by one or more trust anchor managers, and a device may have more than one store, each used by one or more applications. A trust anchor manager is the entity responsible for managing the contents of a store, and each one is assumed to be represented as, or delegated by, a distinct trust anchor. An application may use several stores, and a store may be used by several applications.

Where this is used: verifying signatures on firmware packages loaded into hardware modules such as cryptographic modules, cable boxes and routers, which are often managed remotely and must be able to authenticate the source of management interactions; web browsers, which use trust anchors to authenticate web servers; and email clients, which use them to validate signed email and to authenticate recipients of encrypted email.
sections.plainLanguage: A trust anchor is a public key that a device has been told to trust, together with rules about what that key may be trusted for.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
Most Internet browsers and email clients use trust anchors when authenticating TLS sessions, verifying signed email and generating encrypted email. Many software distributions are digitally signed so that the source can be authenticated before installation. The trust anchors supporting these applications are typically installed with the operating system or application, installed by an enterprise configuration management system, or installed directly by the user. They are usually kept in application-specific or operating-system-specific stores, and a single machine may hold several stores that are not synchronised. Reviewing the contents of one store typically means using a proprietary tool that talks to that kind of store.

The presence of a trust anchor in a store often conveys implicit authorisation to validate signatures for any context from which the store is accessed. The public key of a timestamp authority may sit in a trust anchor store to validate signatures on timestamps, but if that store is shared by applications serving different purposes, the same key may inappropriately be used to validate other kinds of object such as certificates or OCSP responses. Before the publication of RFC 5914 there was no standard general-purpose way to limit the scope of a trust anchor, and the common workaround was to put different trust anchors in different stores and limit which applications could reach each store.

Trust relationships between public key infrastructures are negotiated by policy authorities, and those negotiations often take a long time so that all the parties' requirements are met. Those requirements are expressed, to some extent, in certificates through policy constraints and name constraints. For them to be enforced, trust anchor stores must be managed in line with what the policy authority intended. Otherwise the constraints in a cross-certificate could be circumvented by treating the subject of that cross-certificate as a trust anchor itself, which would let path-processing implementations skip the cross-certificate.

Trust anchors are often represented as self-signed certificates, which give no useful way to establish the validity of what the certificate contains. Confidence in a trust anchor's integrity is typically established out of band, often by checking the fingerprint, a one-way hash, of the self-signed certificate with an authoritative source. Routine rekeying needs similar out-of-band checks, though in-band rekey of a trust anchor is supported by the Certificate Management Protocol. Ideally only the initial set of trust anchors installed in a store should need out-of-band verification, particularly where the cost of such checks is high relative to the security requirements of the applications using the store.

Despite all this, there is neither a standard way to discover which trust anchors are installed in a given store nor a standard way of managing them. The rest of the document describes the requirements for a solution to that problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Every device keeps its own list of trusted keys, and today there is no standard way to find out what is in that list or to update it. Because the list is shared between applications, a key trusted for one job can end up trusted for another.

sections.title: Transport Independence and the Basic Operations
sections.content:
A general-purpose solution for managing trust anchors must be transport independent so that it applies to a range of device communications environments. It must work in both session-oriented and store-and-forward environments, and in both push and pull distribution models. To accommodate both communication models uniformly, connectionless integrity and data origin authentication for trust anchor transactions must be provided at the application layer; confidentiality may be provided for such transactions. The reason for connectionless integrity alone is that some devices that use trust anchors are not available for online management and may need manual interaction, and because only connectionless integrity is required for compatibility with store-and-forward contexts.

At a minimum, a protocol used for trust anchor management must let a trust anchor manager do four things: determine which trust anchors are installed in a particular store, add one or more trust anchors to a store, remove one or more trust anchors from a store, and replace an entire store. A protocol must provide support for these basic operations, but not every implementation has to support every option; some may support only replacement of whole stores. The RFC notes that an edit operation was left out for simplicity, with a remove followed by an add used instead, and that a single add or remove can act on more than one trust anchor to avoid unnecessary round trips.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol must work over any kind of link, whether the device is online or not, and whether the keys are pushed to it or it asks for them. And it must be able to do four basic things: list, add, remove and replace.

sections.title: Management Targets and Delegation
sections.content:
A protocol for trust anchor management must let a transaction be aimed at all the stores the manager is responsible for, at an enumerated list of one or more named groups of stores, or at an individual store.

Connections between public key infrastructures can be made in different ways: unilateral or bilateral cross-certification, or a community may simply elect to accept a trust anchor from another community. These decisions usually happen at the enterprise level, but in some scenarios it is useful to make such connections for a small community inside an enterprise. Enterprise-wide mechanisms such as cross-certificates are ill-suited to this, because certificate revocation or expiration affects the whole enterprise. A trust anchor management protocol can address this by supporting limited installation of trust anchors, that is, installing them in subsets of the enterprise user community, and by supporting the expression of constraints on how relying parties may use a trust anchor. Limited installation needs the ability to identify the members of the community meant to rely on a particular trust anchor, and the ability to query and report on store contents. Trust anchor configurations may be uniform across an enterprise or unique to a single application or small set of applications, and many devices and some applications use several stores, so addressing a specific store or a collection of them lets one manager keep control of all of them efficiently.

The protocol must also let control of a trust anchor store be transferred securely from one trust anchor manager to another, and should let a manager delegate specific operations without handing over the overall management capability. Trust anchor manager rekey is one kind of transfer that must be supported, in which the new key is given the same privileges as the old one. Creating trust anchors for a specific purpose, such as firmware signing, is another example of delegation: a manager may delegate only the authority to sign firmware while disallowing further delegation of that privilege, or may let its delegate delegate the firmware signing authority on to other entities.
sections.plainLanguage: A transaction can be aimed at one store, at a named group of stores, or at everything the manager is responsible for. And a manager can hand a store to another manager, or lend just one job, such as signing firmware, and decide whether the borrower may pass it on.

sections.title: What a Trust Anchor Must Be Able to Say
sections.content:
The protocol must manage trust anchors that will be used to validate certification paths and certificate revocation lists in accordance with RFC 5280 and RFC 5055. The trust anchor format must be able to represent constraints that influence certification path validation or otherwise establish the scope of use of the trust anchor's public key; examples are name constraints, certificate policies and key usage. Certification path validation is one of the most common uses of trust anchors, and the rules for using them for path validation are set out in RFC 5280. Trust anchors used for path validation are responsible for providing, possibly through a delegate, the revocation status of the certificates they issue, which is often done by signing a revocation list.

The protocol must also manage trust anchors used for purposes other than certification path validation, including ones that cannot be used for path validation at all. It should be possible to authorise a trust anchor to delegate authority to other trust anchors or certificate holders, and to prevent one from delegating authority. Trust anchors validate a variety of signed objects, not just certificates and revocation lists: a trust anchor may verify firmware packages, OCSP responses, SCVP responses or timestamps. A trust anchor authorised for some or all of these may not be authorised to verify public key certificates or revocation lists, so it matters to be able to impose constraints on the ways a given trust anchor is employed.

Minimally, the protocol must support trust anchors represented as self-signed certificates and as a distinguished name, public key information and, optionally, associated data. The definition of a trust anchor must include a public key, a public key algorithm and, if necessary, public key parameters. When the public key validates certification paths or revocation lists, a distinguished name must also be included, as RFC 5280 requires. The format should enable the specification of a public key identifier so that other applications of the trust anchor can work, for example verifying data signed using the Cryptographic Message Syntax SignedData structure, and should enable the representation of constraints restricting the use of the trust anchor. Before RFC 5914 there was no standardised format for trust anchors: self-signed X.509 certificates are typically used, but RFC 5280 does not mandate a particular representation and requires only that the public key information and distinguished name be available during path validation. Constraints may include a validity period and constraints on certification path validation.
sections.plainLanguage: A trust anchor has to say what it is trusted for, so that a key meant only for checking timestamps cannot be used to check certificates. The format has to carry the key, its algorithm, the name it was issued under, and any limits on its use.

sections.title: Authentication, Replay and Recovery
sections.content:
An entity receiving trust anchor management data must be able to authenticate the identity of the party providing the information and must be able to confirm that the party is authorised to provide it. A trust anchor manager must be able to authenticate which store a report listing the contents belongs to, and to confirm that the contents of the report have not been altered since. Data origin authentication and integrity are needed to support remote management operations, even when the transactions travel over a store-and-forward network.

When performing add operations, the protocol should let a relying party check the integrity of the trust anchor automatically, without relying on out-of-band trust mechanisms. Traditionally a trust anchor is distributed out of band with its integrity checked manually before installation, and installation is typically performed by anyone with enough administrative privilege on the receiving system. Reducing the need for out-of-band mechanisms is one of the main reasons for developing a trust anchor management protocol, and ideally out-of-band mechanisms would be needed only when a store is first initialised.

The protocol must let participants detect replay attacks, and a replay detection mechanism that does not require a reliable source of time must be available; mechanisms that do require one may also be available. Replaying old transactions could reintroduce compromised trust anchors into a store, exposing applications to malicious signed objects or certification paths, and some devices that use trust anchors have no access to a reliable time source, so a mechanism that needs one is not enough.

The protocol must also let a system recover from the compromise or loss of a trust anchor private key, including the private key authorised to act as a trust anchor manager, without re-initialising the trust store. Losing or compromising such a key can have serious consequences, and in some cases today recovery means re-initialising every affected store.

The security considerations add that the public key used to authenticate a transaction may have been placed in the client by an earlier transaction or during initial bootstrap configuration, and that at least one public key authorised for trust anchor management must be in each store so the store can be managed when it is first configured; that key may be transported and checked out of band. Compromise of a trust anchor's private key can cause many problems, including issuing bogus certificates or installing rogue trust anchors. Using constraints needs great care: a typo in a name constraint for a trust anchor that is the root of a public key infrastructure causes denial of service for certificate holders and relying parties, and if a manager inadvertently delegates all of its privileges and the delegate then removes the manager from the stores now under its control, recovery may require re-initialising every affected store. RFC 5280 requires that path validation be initialised with a trust anchor subject name and public key, but does not require processing other information such as name constraint extensions; where constraints are explicitly included there is an expectation that the path validation algorithm will use them, so application owners must confirm that the path processing implementations support TA-based constraints. Many of the security considerations of RFC 5280 also apply here.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver has to know who sent the keys and that they were not changed in transit, old transactions must not be replayable, and there has to be a way back if a key is lost. The RFC also warns that a typo in a constraint can break everything.
